qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Identify two differences between perfect competition and monopoly concerning suppliers and entry.
items.canonical_answer: Perfect competition has many suppliers and free entry; monopoly has a single supplier in the defined market and barriers restricting entry.
marking_guidance: Feature/contrast (1): many suppliers versus one. Distinction (1): free versus restricted entry.
objective_titles: Discuss and evaluate pricing and output policies in perfect competition and monopoly

items.canonical_answer: A model with many price-taking firms selling an identical product, with free entry and exit and adequate information.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): the complete model conditions, including price taking, identical product and entry/information assumptions.
objective_titles: Define perfect competition; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.

items.canonical_answer: A market structure with a single supplier in the defined market and barriers that restrict entry.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): single supplier in the defined market protected by entry barriers.
objective_titles: Define monopoly; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.

items.prompt: Evaluate perfect competition for consumers where its model assumptions hold, but a larger single producer could obtain genuine scale savings.
items.canonical_answer: Many price-taking suppliers and informed choice constrain individual pricing power. However, smaller suppliers may lack the stated scale savings. Prefer the competitive outcome if its price, quality and cost discipline serve consumers better; if a larger supplier passes on sufficient savings while preserving quality, that alternative may improve the comparison. The structure alone does not settle the outcome.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): alternative suppliers/information constrain pricing power (1), consumers can switch from an overpriced identical product (1). Argument against (2): small scale may miss savings (1), raising possible cost relative to a suitable larger producer (1). Condition (1): actual prices/quality and passed-on savings. Judgement (2): conditional preference for competitive consumer outcome (1), recognise a changed price/cost comparison could alter it (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Define perfect competition; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.

items.prompt: Evaluate a monopolist’s lower production cost for consumers. Invented comparison: competitive suppliers have average cost N$9 and price N$10; monopoly has average cost N$6 and price N$12 because it passes little of its scale saving to buyers.
items.canonical_answer: The monopoly’s scale saving reduces stated average cost, offering a potential efficiency benefit. However, buyers pay N$12 instead of N$10, so the actual price comparison is worse for them despite lower cost. Judge the cost gain separately from consumer benefit; consumers benefit if enough savings are passed on with quality maintained, which the stated price does not demonstrate.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): lower average cost N$6 versus N$9 (1), potential efficiency gain from scale (1). Argument against (2): price N$12 versus N$10 (1), savings not sufficiently passed to consumers (1). Condition (1): actual pass-through and quality. Judgement (2): no demonstrated consumer price gain here (1), conditional gain only if price/quality comparison improves (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Define monopoly; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.

items.prompt: Define perfect competition (2). Identify two monopoly characteristics (2). Explain why an individual competitive firm is a price taker under the model assumptions (2). Identify two constraints on monopoly pricing (2).
items.canonical_answer: Perfect competition has many price-taking firms supplying an identical product under free entry/exit and adequate information. Monopoly has a single supplier in the defined market and entry barriers. An overpriced competitive firm can lose buyers to informed alternatives, limiting its individual pricing power. Market demand and production costs constrain the monopolist.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): many price-taking firms/identical product (1), free entry/exit and information assumptions (1). Separate points for monopoly (2): single supplier (1), entry barrier (1). Explanation (2): buyers have informed identical alternatives (1), constraining the firm’s price choice (1). Constraints (2): demand (1), costs (1). Marks allocation 8.
objective_titles: Define perfect competition; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.
Define monopoly; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.

items.prompt: Invented comparison: Case A meets perfect-competition assumptions. Case B has one supplier and an entry barrier. At the compared output, A has average cost N$9 and price N$10; B has average cost N$6 and price N$12. Describe three structural features distinguishing the cases (6). Explain how pricing and output decisions differ, including the role of demand and additional costs/revenue (7). Discuss whether B’s lower cost establishes that it is better for consumers (7).
items.canonical_answer: A has many suppliers of an identical product, free entry and adequate information; B has a single supplier and restricted entry. A firm in A takes the market price and selects output in relation to costs. B faces market demand, so selling more generally requires a price change and its additional revenue can differ from price. Both consider additional revenue and cost for a profit objective under the relevant maximum conditions. B’s lower cost is a potential efficiency advantage, but buyers pay more in the stated comparison. Consumer benefit depends on price, quality and pass-through, not on cost alone.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): many versus single supplier (2); free versus restricted entry (2); informed identical alternatives in A versus absence of another supplier within B’s market (2). Mechanism/explanation (7): competitive price taking (1), informed alternatives constrain deviation (1), additional revenue equals market price in A (1); B faces market demand (1), more output can require lower price (1), additional revenue can be below price (1); output compares additional revenue/cost at a maximum (1). Both sides/judgement (7): B cost N$6 versus N$9 (1), potential efficiency gain (1); B price N$12 versus N$10 (1), worse buyer price despite saving (1); condition pass-through/quality (1); reject automatic consumer benefit (1), reconsider only if actual consumer outcome improves (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.
objective_titles: Define perfect competition; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.
Define monopoly; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.

items.prompt: Evaluate two alternative monopoly outcomes against perfect competition in separate seven-mark plans. Invented Case 1: a large sole producer obtains scale savings and passes enough on to sell below the competitive comparison price, with quality maintained. Case 2: it obtains the same saving but passes little on, charging above the comparison price. Entry is restricted in both cases. Consider efficiency, buyers’ alternatives and the actual price/output policy.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: scale savings lower cost and a lower price can benefit consumers, but restricted entry reduces their alternative suppliers. Conditional support rests on the maintained price/quality advantage. Case 2: cost savings benefit the firm potentially, while buyers face a higher price and weak alternative supply. Prefer the competitive comparison for the stated consumer-price objective unless price or quality evidence changes. Both judgements distinguish a productive advantage from its distribution rather than declaring monopoly always good or always bad.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for lower cost (1), saving reaches consumers through lower price (1); argument against restricted alternatives (1), weak entry pressure (1); condition maintained price/quality gain (1); judgement conditionally favours stated outcome (1), no universal monopoly claim (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for potential efficiency saving (1), firm can use lower cost (1); argument against higher buyer price (1), restricted alternatives (1); condition actual price/quality compared with competition (1); judgement favours competitive consumer comparison here (1), conditional on unchanged evidence (1). Total 14.
objective_titles: Define perfect competition; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.
Define monopoly; discuss and evaluate its pricing and output policies.
